_comment: Mutation gate over the guard scripts. `mutate` names files one by one on purpose: the threshold-ratchet `stryker` family reports a removed mutate target as a weakening, so every guard listed here is protected by name and can only leave through a human-approved thresholdRatchet.allow entry. `thresholds.break` is the measured score of this list, not an aspiration, and the same ratchet forbids lowering it. See wiki/decisions/2026-08-19-guard-mutation-gate.md for the whole contract, including what this cannot reach. NOT every guard: this list is `.mjs` because Stryker's instrumenter is per-language and has NO shell parser, so every guard written in `.sh` is outside this gate BY CONSTRUCTION and no `mutate` pattern can bring it in. Do not add one here to close that gap — measured, Stryker aborts the whole run with `No parser registered for .sh!` and takes every other guard's score with it, which is why `lisa-mutation.mjs` now refuses such an entry as `uninstrumentable-mutate-target`. Shell guards are evidenced by driving tests instead.
_timeoutMSComment: Per-mutant slack, and a liveness bound rather than a performance assertion for the same reason the dry-run budget below is one. Stryker's per-mutant budget is `netTime * timeoutFactor + timeoutMS`, so this is added ON TOP of each mutant's own measured runtime: at 60000 a mutant is only killed by the clock when it runs a full minute beyond what the same test took in the dry run. Stryker's unset default is 5000ms, and a timed-out mutant is scored as KILLED — so leaving it unset would quietly make the score on this list a function of how busy the machine was. Absolute BY DESIGN, not by omission: Stryker's budget is `netTime * timeoutFactor + timeoutMS`, and the SCALING term already exists — `timeoutFactor` (default 1.5) multiplies each mutant's own runtime as measured on the machine actually running it, so machine speed is adapted to before this constant is added. Stryker's own schema calls timeoutMS "an absolute timeout deviation. Tweak this if you run Stryker on a busy machine and you need to wait longer to make sure that the code indeed entered an infinite loop." That is exactly the use here.
_dryRunTimeoutMinutesComment: Stryker's default dryRunTimeoutMinutes cap is 5 minutes. The dry run's own workload was measured at 159s on an idle box — a 1.9x margin, which is the thin-margin anti-pattern this repository has been documenting, sitting in a config file. Under the oversubscription this machine actually sees (loadavg 167 on 18 cores, ~9x) it cannot reach 300s, and every push in the repository fails on it while the hook reports `mutation score below threshold` — false twice over, since no score is computed and no test is weak. This is NOT the budget #2490 warns against turning: that one is vitest's per-test timeout inside a suite that starves its own child, where a longer budget only delays the report because the siblings never yield. This one is a lone subprocess at the push moment competing with other AGENTS, and it does finish given wall clock. A liveness bound, not a performance assertion: a genuinely hung dry run still fails, just later, and CI's job timeout still caps it. Nothing about what the gate proves changes — thresholds.break stays where the ratchet holds it. Absolute BY NECESSITY: this bounds the run that PRODUCES the timing measurement, so there is nothing yet measured to scale it against. It cannot be made adaptive the way a per-mutant budget can. The claim it makes is deliberately weak — not "your dry run finishes in this long" but "a dry run still going at this point is wedged rather than slow" — which is what lets one number hold across hardware nobody here has seen. It fails only where a HEALTHY dry run genuinely exceeds it, which takes a pathological environment rather than a slow one (a saturated temp directory can make a single mkdtemp cost seconds). In that case the environment is the bug and raising this number hides it — which is why the gate now reports a blown budget as `dry-run-timeout` naming this value, rather than as a mutation score.
_cleanTempDirComment: Default `true` removes the sandbox only after a SUCCESSFUL run, so exactly the runs that need investigating are the ones that leave a full second copy of the tree behind — and a leftover sandbox costs the next lint 1191 errors. `always` removes it either way — meaning pass or fail, NOT killed. This is Stryker's own teardown, so a SIGTERM, an OOM reap, a maxBuffer overflow and a Ctrl-C all skip it, and those are the runs a busy machine actually produces; one such kill left 72 MB behind. The gate handles that half rather than this setting: it gives each run its own `.stryker-tmp/run-<pid>-<epoch>` sandbox and reclaims, at the START of the next run, the ones whose owning process is gone. Reclaiming after the fact cannot run in the case that creates the mess, and reclaiming a SHARED path would delete a concurrent run's working directory (#2961).
_ignorePatternsComment: Stryker does NOT read .gitignore; without these it copies dist/ and coverage/ into every sandbox. That is not merely slow — the integration suite rebuilds dist/ while this runs, so the sandbox scan lists .d.ts files that are gone by the time it reads them and the whole gate dies on ENOENT. Nothing in the run needs either: the package self-resolves through the symlinked node_modules to the real checkout.
_thresholdsOwner: Owned by .lisa.config.json quality.mutation.strykerThresholds. Every other key in this file is Stryker's own and is yours to edit; `thresholds` is not. `lisa sync` writes it from that config key, and when the two disagree it does one of two things (src/sync/stryker-thresholds-ownership.ts): with `_thresholdsDivergence` below recording both live numbers and a reason, it proceeds, leaves this value alone, and says it is honouring a recorded divergence; with nothing recording why, it REFUSES and names both values. So change the config, not this line — and if the two must differ for a while, keep `_thresholdsDivergence` current, because a stale block stops exempting anything and fails a test.

_thresholdsDivergence.reason: Neither number is right yet, and that is deliberate (CodySwannGT/lisa#2968). 32 leaves wide slack against a measured ~58 aggregate; 60 fails today and fails harder as CodySwannGT/lisa#2940 lands, because bounding unbounded child spawns reveals mutants currently scored as killed only because they timed out — so the true score is still moving. Sizing a floor against a distribution that is still clipping is the exact defect this campaign has hit repeatedly. Sequence: land the spawn bounding, measure the true aggregate, set BOTH files to one value just below it, delete this block, then ratchet.
